opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the more exciting things happening right now. Creative work is obviously where most people first encountered these models, generating art, illustrations, concept designs, but I think that's really just the most visible tip of it.

One area I'm really interested in is using generative models as a kind of general-purpose visual understanding engine. If a model can generate a realistic image of a scene, it has implicitly learned a lot about how the world looks: geometry, lighting, materials, how objects relate to each other. People are finding you can repurpose those learned representations for things like depth estimation, segmentation, or relighting, often with surprisingly little extra training. So the generative model becomes a foundation for perception tasks, not just synthesis.

Another big one is synthetic data. In robotics, autonomous driving, or medical imaging, collecting and labeling real data is expensive, and sometimes the rare cases you care most about barely show up in your dataset. Being able to generate realistic, controllable variations, different weather, different lighting, unusual edge cases, can help train and stress-test downstream systems. There are real caveats about distribution shift and making sure you're not baking in artifacts, but the potential is significant.

Then there's what I'd call practical editing and communication: product visualization for e-commerce, interior design previews, helping someone see what a renovation might look like, or educational content where you illustrate a concept on the fly. These aren't art in the traditional sense, they're tools for communicating visually when you don't have the skills or time to make the image yourself.

And looking a bit further out, the line between image generation and video and world modeling is blurring. Once you can generate coherent sequences that respect physics and cause and effect, you're getting close to simulators that agents could use to plan or learn. That's still early, but I think it's where a lot of the most interesting research is heading.

Of course, all of this comes with responsibilities around provenance, misuse, and making sure people can tell what's real. That's something the field has to take seriously as these models move into more consequential settings. But overall, I see image generation becoming less of a novelty and more of a core building block for how machines understand and interact with the visual world.

r001.rationale: It says creative work was where most people first encountered the models, but does not explain that creative applications tolerate imperfect outputs.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison to the early GPT-1 and GPT-2 period or its predominantly creative experimentation.

r003.rationale: It mentions visual communication and educational content, but does not connect image generation to the visual aspects of seeking information or working through problems.

r004.rationale: It discusses realistic images and cautions about artifacts, but does not identify improved factuality or reliability as what enables expansion beyond creative applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because when people hear "image generation" they tend to picture someone typing a prompt and getting a pretty picture back, and that's obviously a big part of it. But I actually think the more interesting stuff over the next few years is going to be in places that don't look like art at all.

One way I frame it is that these models have learned a really rich prior about how the visual world is structured. Lighting, materials, geometry, how objects relate to each other, what things look like from different angles. And once you have that prior, generation is just one thing you can do with it. You can also use it to fill in missing information, to simulate, to edit, to reason about images in ways that used to require a whole pipeline of hand-built tools.

So take something like photography on a phone. A lot of what's happening there already is generative in spirit. Low-light enhancement, super-resolution, removing an object from the background, relighting a portrait after the fact. The user doesn't think of that as "AI art," they think of it as their camera being good. And I think that's the pattern. The successful uses outside creative work are the ones where the model disappears into a tool and the person just gets a better result.

Another area I'm really excited about is anything where you need data that's expensive or impossible to capture. Robotics is a good example. You want to train a system on a huge variety of environments, lighting conditions, object placements, and you can't physically go collect all of that. Being able to synthesize plausible, controllable variations of real scenes is genuinely useful there. Same thing in medical imaging for augmentation, or in autonomous driving for rare edge cases that you'd never want to encounter on a real road.

Then there's the design and engineering side. Architects, product designers, people doing interior layouts. For them it's less about making a finished image and more about rapidly exploring a space of options. What does this room look like with the window moved? What if the material on this chair were different? Historically that's a render cycle that takes hours. If it takes seconds, the way you work changes. You iterate more, you consider ideas you'd otherwise have thrown out because they weren't worth the effort to visualize.

And honestly, I think one of the biggest shifts is that the line between generation and understanding is blurring. The same models that can produce an image are increasingly the ones that can look at an image and reason about it. So you end up with systems that can take a photo of your broken bike, show you what the fixed version should look like, and explain the steps. Or take a messy whiteboard sketch and turn it into a clean diagram. That's not really "creative work" in the traditional sense, it's communication, it's instruction, it's problem solving with pictures.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming it's going to be one big killer app. I think it's going to be a thousand small things, each one a little boring on its own, where a visual model quietly makes some task faster or possible. That's usually how transformative technology actually shows up.

r001.rationale: It says creative work is a major use, but does not explain that creative applications came early because they tolerate imperfect outputs.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison to the early GPT-1 and GPT-2 period.

r003.rationale: It describes using images to explain how to fix a bike and turn a sketch into a diagram, framing these as communication and problem solving with pictures.

r004.rationale: It does not say improved factuality or reliability enables uses beyond creative applications.

astra-6.text:
I think one interesting direction is using image generation as a way to learn about the visual world. To generate a plausible image, a model has to capture something about objects, their relationships, and how scenes are structured. The question is whether we can use what it learns for tasks beyond making pictures—for example, helping a system interpret a scene or supplying training data for another model.

Synthetic data is particularly interesting when collecting real examples is expensive or when the situations you care about are rare. You could generate variations in lighting, environments, or object configurations and use those to train and test perception systems. But you have to verify that the generated data actually improves performance in the real world. A convincing image isn’t necessarily an accurate training example.

So I see the potential extending into vision and robotics, where generation could help systems reason about what they might see or what might happen next. That’s a harder requirement than producing something visually appealing, but it’s an exciting direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the really interesting directions is using image generation as a way to understand the world, beyond producing something visually compelling. If a model can generate plausible images of a scene under different conditions, can we use that capability to reason about the scene or help another system learn from it?

For example, you could generate training data for situations that are difficult to capture in the real world. In robotics, that might mean showing an object in different environments or exploring what a scene could look like after an action. The challenge is that a plausible image isn’t necessarily a physically correct one. So the question becomes how to make these models reliable enough that their outputs are useful for learning and decision-making.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison to the early GPT-1/GPT-2 period or to predominantly creative experimentation.

r003.rationale: It discusses reasoning about scenes and generating robotics training data, but does not identify visual communication as supporting information seeking or problem solving.

r004.rationale: It says plausible images may not be physically correct and that models must become reliable enough for their outputs to support learning and decision-making, linking reliability to broader uses beyond creative work.
